/ Why it matters

Upstream stages are
hard to see.

Rare earth supply is concentrated, and the further back you go, the less a finished-part declaration usually says. That is why evidence for earlier stages takes time to gather.

Upstream stages come into scope

From 1 January 2027 the clause reaches mining, refining and separation, not only melting and production. See sources.

/ The rule

What the clause
looks at.

DFARS 252.225-7052 restricts delivery to the Department of Defense of certain magnets (NdFeB and SmCo), tungsten and tantalum, and of end items containing them, where covered stages took place in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. Through 31 December 2026 it covers material melted or produced in those countries. From 1 January 2027 it also covers material mined, refined or separated there. The clause includes exceptions, and contractors are expected to include it in qualifying subcontracts.

It can reach lower tiers

Primes and higher-tier suppliers may flow the clause down and ask for supporting information about origin.

Earlier stages need records

Separation and metal-making are often several tiers away from you. Records for those stages usually have to be requested, not found.

Waivers are tightening

A July 2026 executive order directs DoD to stop issuing certain waivers for covered materials from 1 January 2027. See sources.

/ How we work

How an engagement
runs.

  1. 01

    Agree the scope

    We agree which parts and suppliers are included, the timeline and a fixed fee before any work begins.

  2. 02

    Map the parts

  3. 03

    Request documents

  4. 04

    Review by stage

    Each document is matched to the production stage it describes, with its date and issuer recorded.

  5. 05

    Mark the gaps

    Stages with no document, unclear wording, or a covered country are listed in plain English with the question to ask.

  6. 06

    Hand over the pack

    You receive an evidence pack for your own review and for the questions your customer may ask.

/ FAQ

Common
questions.

Does this rule apply to my company?

It may, if your products reach the Department of Defense, directly or through a prime, and contain NdFeB or SmCo magnets, tungsten or tantalum. Whether it applies, and whether an exception is available, depends on the specific contract and the responsible reviewer. A readiness call can help you work out which questions to ask.

We already have a supplier declaration. Isn't that enough?

It depends on what it says. Many declarations describe the finished part or the magnet maker only. From 1 January 2027 the clause also looks at mining, refining and separation, so it helps to know which stages your documents actually cover.

Does recycled material count?

It depends on the material and the stage. From 1 January 2027 the clause's upstream restriction refers to ore and feedstock, including recycled material, for several covered materials, so where recycled feed came from can matter. The statute also contains a narrow exception for NdFeB magnets made from recycled material when milling and sintering take place in the United States, and some later statutory changes may not yet appear in the DFARS clause. Whether any exception applies to your parts is a question for the contract and the responsible reviewer.

How long does a pilot take?

Most of the time goes into waiting for supplier responses. We agree a timeline as part of the scope before work begins.

What if a stage shows a covered country or has no document?

The evidence pack says so plainly, names the document (or the lack of one), and lists the question to put to the supplier. What happens next is a decision for you, your customer and the responsible reviewer.

Do you need our drawings or controlled data?

No. We work from part numbers, material descriptions and supplier origin documents. Please do not send drawings, controlled technical data, contract files or export-controlled information.

Is this legal advice or a certification?

No. Lodeline provides supply-chain documentation and analysis, not legal advice or government certification. Applicability, exceptions, and acceptance depend on the contract and the responsible reviewer.
